title: ASFA sharpens implementation focus with chief practice officer
full_text:
The Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia (ASFA) has appointed Sarah O’Brien as chief practice officer and head of ASFA InPractice, with her tenure beginning on 21 September.
O’Brien will join ASFA from industry super fund Rest, where she served as head of regulatory policy after previously working as general manager, regulatory and technical services.
Her more than two decades of experience in super regulation and implementation has also included senior roles at Commonwealth Bank and Colonial First State.
Between 2016 and 2019, O’Brien served as executive officer and company secretary of the Gateway Network Governance Body (GNGB), which oversees the integrity and security of the superannuation transaction network. She is also a member of the Women in Super national policy committee.
The appointment follows ASFA’s decision in May to expand ASFA InPractice, its service supporting funds, administrators and other providers through regulatory change and implementation.
Beginning this financial year, the service has become available to all funds through their ASFA membership, extending its involvement from the early stages of policymaking through to practical implementation.
O’Brien will take over the executive leadership of the Superannuation Cyber and Financial Crime Coordination Framework, which coordinates the sector’s response to cybercrime, fraud and scams.
Her immediate priorities will also include third-party vendor mapping under CPS 230, providing funds with a shared view of the service provider dependencies they are required to identify and manage.
APRA and ASIC have recently warned that shared dependencies could allow isolated incidents to develop into sector-wide disruption, identifying industry-led dependency mapping as part of the response to emerging risks.
O’Brien will also oversee the ASFA InPractice community of practice focused on the responsible adoption and oversight of artificial intelligence in superannuation.
The group is developing an AI governance guide, an AI risk management guide and regulatory readiness framework, and a use case classification guide. The resources are intended to support trustees, directors and executives as AI adoption accelerates.
ASFA chief executive Mary Delahunty said implementation practitioners played an important role in translating system changes into fund operations.
“System change doesn’t finish when the headlines about new super legislation are published. That’s when the most complex and costly work begins, working out how new regulations and guidance translate into day-to-day business,” Delahunty said.
“It’s crucial that ASFA guides this work as the peak body for the sector, and that the person providing that guidance has decades of unrivalled hands-on experience inside super.
“There are few people who understand both the regulatory intent and the reality of implementing change inside a fund as well as Sarah does. She knows where greater coordination can take unnecessary complexity and cost out of the system.”
O’Brien said growing scrutiny from the government and regulators, alongside rising member expectations, had made implementation a priority across the super industry.
“I have participated across ASFA’s fund community and working groups for many years. ASFA InPractice is a unique space, bringing together a non-competitive community of practitioners across funds, administrators and service providers, and I’m excited to now be leading that work as a part of the ASFA team,” O’Brien said.
“Our job is to encourage a consistent, compliant approach to implementation across the sector. That is about making design choices centred on managing risk and protecting the security of Australians’ retirement savings.
“When the sector is getting implementation right across the board, every fund’s members win. I’m looking forward to working with ASFA funds to deliver for the millions of Australians they represent.”
